sections.category: Microsoft's Azure quarter and Meta's cash-flow quarter split the AI-capex trade in opposite directions on the same tape

bullets.body: Microsoft reported fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, July 29, and the market re-rated the stock on Thursday, July 30. Revenue was $90.0 billion, up 18%, operating income $40.6 billion, also up 18%, net income $35.8 billion and diluted earnings per share $4.81 on a reported basis and $4.74 excluding a one-off, against a Street estimate nearer $4.24. The line that moved the price was Azure and other cloud services revenue up 43%, and Satya Nadella's statement that Azure revenue passed $100 billion for the first time in a fiscal year. Microsoft Cloud revenue was $59.3 billion, up 27%, the Intelligent Cloud segment $39.3 billion, up 32%, Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats and GitHub Copilot 50 million users. Capital expenditure including finance leases was $41 billion in the quarter, roughly two thirds of it on short-lived assets — the processors and accelerators absorbing customer demand — and Microsoft brought up 31 datacentres across five continents in the quarter and 88 across the fiscal year. Chief financial officer Amy Hood guided first-quarter capital spend above $50 billion and first-quarter Azure growth of approximately 45% in constant currency, said demand continues to exceed available supply, and disclosed an accounting change that matters to the capex headline: the estimated useful life of datacentres and office buildings is being extended from 15 to 25 years at the start of fiscal 2027, which pushes more leases from finance to operating treatment and, because capital expenditure counts finance leases but not operating ones, lowers the calendar-2026 capital expenditure expectation to roughly $175 billion while leaving the underlying investment unchanged.

bullets.body: Meta reported the same evening and drew the opposite verdict. Revenue was $60.801 billion, up 28% and ahead of consensus, but total costs and expenses rose 55% to $42.026 billion, income from operations fell 8% to $18.775 billion, the operating margin compressed to 31% from 43% a year earlier, net income fell 14% to $15.848 billion and diluted earnings per share fell 13% to $6.18. The number that did the damage sits below that: capital expenditure of $31.08 billion in the quarter cut free cash flow to $784 million. Meta narrowed its full-year 2026 capital expenditure outlook from $125-145 billion to $130-145 billion — a lift at the floor, not a cut at the ceiling — and guided third-quarter revenue to $61-64 billion, a midpoint under the Street. Headcount was 75,472, down 1% from a year earlier. The tape sorted the two accordingly: The Motley Fool's midday snapshot at 12:13 PM ET on Thursday had the Nasdaq Composite up 2.44%, the S&P 500 up 1.29%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.85%, technology up 4.31% as a sector and Microsoft up 15.5%. A separate July 30 market report puts Microsoft up 15.2% and Meta down 8.9% on the session, with the semiconductor complex riding Microsoft's coat-tails — Lam Research up 20.9%, Micron up 15.45%, AMD up 7.3% and Arm up 7.1% — against Qualcomm down 2.8%, while second-quarter gross domestic product growth came in at 1.5%, below forecast, and core personal consumption expenditure inflation at 3.3%, softer than expected, with the Federal Reserve holding rates.

sections.category: Samsung books an all-time-high quarter on server memory, ships what it calls the industry's first HBM4E samples, and watches its own handset unit fall into the red

bullets.body: Samsung Electronics announced second-quarter results on Thursday, July 30: consolidated revenue of KRW 171.5 trillion, up 28% from the first quarter and an all-time high, operating profit of KRW 89.5 trillion, also an all-time high, and earnings per share of KRW 10,849, up 52%. The Device Solutions division is the whole story — revenue of KRW 127.5 trillion and operating profit of KRW 89.2 trillion on sales up 56% quarter on quarter. The Memory Business attributes its record to prioritising server products under limited capacity, which took its share of server revenue to a record high; it scaled up HBM4 sales and shipped what it describes as the industry's first HBM4E samples to major customers. The contrast inside the same company is the part worth holding onto: the Mobile eXperience and Networks businesses posted an operating loss of KRW 0.7 trillion, with revenue up year on year on Galaxy S26 and Galaxy A sales but earnings down on elevated component cost pressure across the industry — the memory cycle paying the Device Solutions division is the same cycle charging Samsung's handset unit. For the second half Samsung expects robust server-led demand from continued AI infrastructure capital expenditure and broader adoption of agentic AI, with growth in server DRAM, enterprise SSD and HBM accelerating and the market staying undersupplied even as mobile and PC demand partially moderates. Trade coverage of the print puts operating profit up 1,813.8% against the same quarter of 2025 and makes this the third quarter running in which Samsung has set an operating-profit record.

sections.category: A maximum-severity flaw in an agent-orchestration harness left 233 privileged tools reachable over HTTP with no password at all

bullets.body: Noma Labs disclosed CVE-2026-59726, which it named RufRoot, on Wednesday, July 29, with the trade write-ups following on Thursday, July 30; it carries the maximum CVSS score of 10.0. The affected project is Ruflo, an open-source multi-agent orchestration platform that began life as Claude Flow and now serves as a harness for Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex, with more than 66,500 GitHub stars. The defect sits in its Model Context Protocol bridge, an Express.js server that brokers every tool invocation across agent workflows. That bridge's POST /mcp endpoint had no authentication, and the shipped docker-compose configuration bound port 3001 to 0.0.0.0, so a default self-hosted deployment published 233 high-privilege tools — shell command execution, database operations, agent management and memory storage — to anyone who could reach the port. A single unauthenticated HTTP request invoking the terminal-execution tool runs commands inside the container; from there an attacker can read stored user conversations, lift the environment variables holding model API keys, reach a MongoDB instance that was running without authentication, spawn agent swarms billed to the victim's own keys, and write poisoned patterns into the AgentDB learning store so that the outputs served to every other user of that deployment are tainted. Noma's framing is that the bridge is not an auxiliary debug interface but the platform's central nervous system, controlling all tool calls and agent actions. Maintainer Reuven Cohen shipped version 3.16.3 within 24 hours of the June 30 responsible disclosure, binding the bridge to loopback, requiring a bearer token, gating terminal execution behind explicit opt-in, enabling MongoDB authentication and tightening container and cross-origin controls. The half of the problem that does not patch away is the memory poisoning: Amit Jena, an AI development manager at Kanerika quoted in CSO Online's coverage, argues that adoption of the protocol has outrun the security defaults built into orchestration tooling, and that poisoned agent memory is not a product-specific failure.

sections.category: Palo Alto Networks documents an operator running an intrusion campaign on an open-weight model through an agent framework, where the machine ran the whole attack workflow by itself and every exploit it attempted failed

bullets.body: Unit 42 published on Thursday, July 30 a reconstruction of a campaign in which an operator tracked as knaithe, also seen as KnYuan and based in Zhuhai, wired DeepSeek into the Hermes Agent framework and drove it from Telegram as an autonomous offensive operator. The observed autonomous phase ran in early May 2026. The agent enumerated vulnerabilities across ten product families, pulled proof-of-concept code from GitHub, ran FOFA queries to find live targets, checked their versions and form endpoints, and then attempted exploitation itself. Unit 42's own conclusion is that this confirms a functional, end-to-end autonomous offensive capability: the machine completed the sequence with no human in it, whatever became of the individual attempts. Seven vulnerabilities were in scope, and the split between what the machine did and what the human did is the finding. The agent tried Langflow's CVE-2026-33017 at CVSS 9.8 and the n8n pair CVE-2026-21858 and CVE-2025-68613 at 10.0 and 9.9 on its own, and failed on all of them — and Unit 42 records why. Against Langflow the agent noted it needed a public flow identifier but found no automatic login and stopped; against n8n it needed an unauthenticated form accepting file upload and found authentication enabled on the forms it reached. Both autonomous failures were defeated by an authentication default being on, which is the same control Ruflo's Model Context Protocol bridge shipped without. The confirmed compromises were manual: three data exfiltrations through Citrix NetScaler's CVE-2026-3055 at 9.8, and command execution on 11 Marimo Notebook instances through CVE-2026-39987 at 9.8. Attempts against Apache Tomcat's CVE-2026-34486 at 7.5 and a Windows IKE VPN flaw, CVE-2026-33824 at 9.8, went nowhere, and a PAN-OS proof of concept for CVE-2026-0300 was cloned but never worked. The target arithmetic is worth keeping: FOFA showed 647,017 n8n instances worldwide and 25,209 inside China, the agent sampled roughly 100 of the Chinese ones and probed about 40 unique addresses, and across more than 460 targeted systems Unit 42 counts three confirmed exploitations — a total its own instance-level figures do not cleanly reconcile with. Model selection was deliberate and it is the part with the longest shelf life. The operator used Claude Code for connectivity and proxy validation and left Codex traces in the exploit-development directories, though Unit 42 could not recover those chat logs because response storage was disabled; the operator evaluated Qwen, GLM, Kimi and MiniMax, and ran the campaign itself on DeepSeek; OpenAI's safety systems refused the requests that violated its policies and disabled an account linked to the activity.

citations.label: Unit 42 - Chinese-speaking threat actor harnesses AI models for autonomous cyberattacks

sections.category: Unsloth spends the day after its release merging fixes, including one that had been silently switching reasoning off on the larger Qwen models

bullets.body: With v0.1.51-beta tagged the previous afternoon and the 2026.7.6 wheel published, Unsloth added no new release tag on Thursday, July 30 and instead merged a run of fixes straight into main. Pull request 7289 is the substantive one. Multi-turn conversations with Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 were losing reasoning content between turns because the ChatMessage model had no reasoning_content field, so Pydantic dropped it silently before the request ever reached the inference server; the same change fixes a size-detection bug that read Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as a 3-billion-parameter model by matching the active-expert count instead of the total, which switched reasoning off on the larger models outright. The fix adds the field, replaces the size extraction with an anchored pattern that scans path segments from the right, teaches truncation to clip reasoning content when the context overflows, and emits an empty content field on reasoning-only assistant turns for llama.cpp compatibility, with 12,583 backend tests passing against a single pre-existing failure and 32 on the frontend. Pull request 7631 closes a genuinely dangerous default: uninstall.sh and uninstall.ps1 ignored their arguments entirely, so a --help flag or a mistyped option uninstalled the product, and the shell script could partially execute if a curl-to-shell stream was truncated mid-download. The uninstallers now print usage and remove nothing on a help flag, name the offending argument and exit non-zero on an unknown one, and remove nothing at all on truncated input, verified across 25 shell and 39 PowerShell argument tests plus 82 more covering shared icons and pipe safety. Pull request 7645 routes six explicit Vulkan setup failures in the Studio setup scripts through the failure helpers rather than bare exits, so a user who asked for Vulkan and hit a failure now sees the error in Studio desktop instead of a silent stop, with 26 shell installer test files clean and 1,387 Python tests passing.

Unsloth pull request 7631 - uninstaller rejects unrecognized arguments instead of uninstalling
Unsloth pull request 7645 - route explicit Vulkan setup failures through the failure helpers

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body:
Two deadlines land within 24 hours of each other. The supplementary video for IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026 is due today, Thursday, July 30, behind the paper submission that closed on Monday, July 27; the next item on that conference's calendar is the workshop and competition proposal deadline on Monday, August 3, then competition decisions on September 21, workshop and tutorial decisions on September 28, paper acceptance notifications on October 6, early-bird registration closing October 16 and camera-ready papers on October 26, with the conference itself in Santa Clara from December 6 to 9 — public forums on the 6th, workshops and tutorials on the 7th, paper sessions on the 8th and 9th. One day out is Hot Chips 2026: the early registration rate closes at 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31, refunds are accepted less a $25 processing fee until 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19, and the symposium runs Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 at Memorial Auditorium at Stanford in Palo Alto, its Sunday tutorial day split between memory technology from 9:00 AM to 12:30 PM — AI data requirements, evolving memory architectures, HBM, advanced packaging and 3D DRAM accelerators — and RISC-V from 1:45 to 5:00 PM. After those, the nearest open deadline is Friday, August 7, when SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit steps its full-conference rate from $1,895 to $2,195.

On the silicon track, FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage takes the Santa Clara Convention Center and the Hyatt Regency from August 4 to 6 with more than 350 speakers, among them NVIDIA vice president of storage technology Jason Hardy, Samsung flash product and technology head Jin-Yub Lee, Micron core data-centre general manager Jeremy Werner and SK hynix solution development head Chunsung Kim. The AI Infra Summit returns to the same Santa Clara hall from September 15 to 17. Further out sit the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose on September 16, the OCP Global Summit from October 12 to 15 in San Jose, NVIDIA's GTC Berlin from October 20 to 22 and SC26 in Chicago from November 15 to 20, with GTC not returning to San Jose until March 2027.

The security track fills the next fortnight. Black Hat USA runs August 1 to 6 at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas — trainings August 1 to 4, six summits on Tuesday, August 4 including the one-day AI Summit, and briefings on August 5 and 6. DEF CON 34 follows August 6 to 9, with the AI Village in Room W603 on Level 1 of the Las Vegas Convention Center, open 10 AM to 5 PM daily; the programme is 12 Creator Stage talks, 20 posters, six fireside chats and two competitions, of which HalCTF — the capture-the-flag where the entrant's agent touches the targets and the entrant never does — is named and the second is still unannounced, with six posters published so far on topics including agent-to-agent worm propagation and prompt exfiltration. Closest to home, the AI Risk Summit takes the Ritz-Carlton at Half Moon Bay, roughly 20 miles from San Francisco International, on August 11 and 12, its full-conference rate stepping from $1,895 to $2,195 after Friday, August 7; the pass covers the co-located CISO Forum Summer Summit, a welcome reception on Monday, August 10, a VIP dinner over the bay on Tuesday, August 11, meals across both days and an optional golf tournament on Thursday, August 13 subject to availability. The AI Security Summit's San Francisco flagship is Thursday, October 15, one day and two tracks, with talk submissions open through Sessionize; its Nordics and Sydney editions are slotted for September with the Nordics host city still unnamed, and the 75-plus speakers, 45-plus sessions and 500-plus attendees the organisers advertise are season totals across all five 2026 editions rather than San Francisco figures. The 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security meets Sunday, November 15 in The Hague alongside the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security; its paper deadline closed firm on July 24, reviews are due September 7, notifications go out September 9 and camera-ready is firm on September 16. Booking further ahead: Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit is in London on October 8 and New York on October 21, with an Asia edition announced but undated and the San Francisco date of May 27 already past; SANS runs its AI Cybersecurity Summit on November 2 and 3 at the Hilton Arlington Rosslyn, hybrid, at $525 for the summit alone, with a $229 room block closing October 9 and a refund cutoff of October 14; and OWASP Global AppSec USA takes the Hyatt Regency San Francisco on November 5 and 6 with hands-on training from November 2 to 4.

New to this list: CoreWeave's Fully Connected lands at Moscone South in San Francisco from September 29 to October 1, and its early-bird rate lapsed yesterday — the standard pass is $1,299 from today, against $899 before. Three tracks cover AI infrastructure, model advances and agent evaluation and monitoring, and the keynote roster runs to CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator and chief technology officer Peter Salanki, NVIDIA vice president and general manager Ian Buck, Fei-Fei Li of Stanford and World Labs, Sarah Guo of Conviction and Liquid AI chief operating officer Jeffrey Li. That puts three San Francisco events on the same three days, because The AI Conference is at Pier 48 Sheds A and B from September 29 to October 1 — five tracks, 5,500-plus attendees, its September 29 workshops and Hack Day capped at 350 and sold out, with two-day pass holders promised first notice if inventory reopens — and OpenAI's DevDay is at Fort Mason on September 29 with applications already closed. Ray Summit is at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis from August 24 to 26, a training day on Monday the 24th and two days of keynotes and breakouts, at $400 for the summit and $450 with training, with the co-located vLLM Conference hosted by Inferact included in the pass and keynotes from Anyscale co-founders Robert Nishihara and Ion Stoica, NVIDIA vice president Bryan Catanzaro, Torc's Felix Heide and Lila Sciences chief technology officer Andrew Beam. AGNTCon and MCPCon North America is October 22 and 23 at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center under the Linux Foundation, built around the Model Context Protocol, agent infrastructure and the security and observability of production agent systems; its call for proposals closed on June 7, so what is left is attendance. Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit is Tuesday, September 29 in San Francisco with applications open, and its Cerebral Valley AI Summit returns to San Francisco on November 12. Ai4 is at The Venetian in Las Vegas from August 4 to 6. The rest of the run: the ACM AI Leadership Summit in Atlanta from August 30 to September 2, the Runway AI Summit on September 30, World Summit AI in Amsterdam on October 7 and 8, the PyTorch Conference in San Jose on October 20 and 21, GitHub Universe at Fort Mason on October 28 and 29, the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco from November 11 to 13 with speaker submissions closing October 11, AWS re:Invent from November 30 to December 4, NeurIPS in December and The AI Summit New York on December 9 and 10.

On AI Tinkerers, the global calendar's near-term listing again carries nothing in San Francisco, Palo Alto or San Jose — the nearest entries are New York on August 1, Seattle on August 4 and Los Angeles on August 6 — and the Palo Alto chapter page refused the connection again today, so the Palo Alto meetup carried here for Tuesday, August 18, 6:30 to 9 PM PDT, apply-to-attend with roughly 150 places and Dyssonance AI sponsoring, stays unconfirmed at source for a second day; San Jose has now appeared alongside Palo Alto and Pleasanton in the calendar's Bay Area chapter list, but with no dated meetup behind it yet. The San Francisco August 9 listing that keeps surfacing in search resolves to an old page, and August 9 falls on a Sunday this year, so it stays closed. Nothing else carried onto this list has passed its end date, so nothing is dropped today.
